newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: First Europeso bonds showcase confidence in Manila.
newsitem.headline: First Europeso bonds showcase confidence in Manila.

text.p: This week's launch of the first-ever peso-denominated Eurobonds reinforces high investor confidence in the Philippines, and more Europeso issues are likely to follow, bankers said on Thursday.
Three days after the International Finance Corp (IFC) issued the first peso Eurobonds worth 2.6 billion pesos ($98.9 million), the World Bank followed on Thursday with a 3.0 billion peso issue.
The issues have put the Philippine peso on the map of traded international currencies, bankers said.
Both were five-year issues with 10.25 percent coupon rates. Citicorp's Citicorp International lead managed the IFC issues, while Deutsche Morgan Grenfell led the World Bank issue.
Andrew Alcid, director of debt syndications at Citicorp in Manila, told Reuters the IFC issue was sold out and was almost twice oversubsribed. "We can't take any more," he said.
The issue is now trading at a premium to the issue price in the secondary market at 100.80 to 101.30, he said.

"This is a continuing testament to the improvement in sentiment of the market towards the Philippines, especially with respect to the economy, market fundamentals, and currency," Alcid told Reuters Financial Television.
"It's also significant in that it will pave the way for Philippine issuers to tap the international market without the cross-currency risk," he added.
Consuelo Garcia, deputy general manager of ING Bank in Manila, said the acceptance of the Europeso notes shows that investors see little currency risk in the bond issue.
Investors who buy the bond assume the Philippine currency risk but not the credit risk because the bonds carry the triple-A rating of the issuers.

"We expect it (the peso) to slightly depreciate," Garcia said, adding that the currency should experience low volatility. The peso had weakened slightly to 26.288 to the dollar by the end of 1996 from 26.228 at the start of the year. It closed at 26.322 on Wednesday and traded at 26.323 on Thursday.
Bankers and analysts said the peso has been drawing strength from large investment flows and a Central Bank armed with robust international reserves that recently reached $12.05 billion.

The government expects a balance of payments surplus of $2.9 billion at the end of 1997 from an estimated $4.1 billion at the end of 1996 as the trade deficit widens to $13.8 billion from $11.786 billion due to heavy purchases of aircraft and capital equipment.
Gross national product is expected to expand by 7.0 percent to 8.0 percent this year from 6.8 percent last year.
After a series of economic reforms, the Philippines hopes to graduate in June this year from 34 years of guidance from the International Monetary Fund.
ING's Garcia said private Philippine companies, which have previously tapped the Eurobond market for funds, are expected to also issue Europeso notes this year.
But she said they would have to price their issues according to to their higher credit risk.
Standard & Poor's Corp last month raised the Philippines' long-term foreign currency debt to BB-plus from BB. The same rating was also given to two major Philippine companies.
